lesson.subject: literacy
lesson.title: The Persuader's Toolkit
lesson.subtitle: Term 4 Week 3, Session 2
lesson.footer: Persuasive Writing | Year 5/6 Literacy | Week 3 Session 2

plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Level 5: VC2E5LA03 language features of persuasive texts; VC2E5LY08 features used to meet purpose and audience; VC2E5LY10 creating persuasive texts
plan.shape: name, add, remix: four devices named on new examples, added to plain sentences, then remixed into the student's own paragraph, because students overuse one device unless they practise choosing
plan.criticalFeature: a device earns its place only if it moves the reader; name its effect, not just its name
decisionPoints: the choice check: which device makes the reader part of the team?
the exit board: a plain sentence with a device added
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Today: four tools for selling it.
plan.catchUp: Missed Week 2? Use the Plastic straws claim from the board as their paragraph to remix instead of their own.

studentTools: Writing books with the Week 2 Prove it paragraph
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: Four devices numbered on the board: 1 rhetorical question, 2 rule of three, 3 repetition, 4 we-words
A spare paragraph for catch-up: Plastic straws harm sea animals. We should stop using them.

slides.notes: Open the session. One line: today we fill our persuader's toolkit with four tools that move a reader.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for those who need it. Number the four devices on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to use persuasive devices on purpose to move a reader.
successCriteria: I can spot four persuasive devices.
I can add a device to make a sentence more persuasive.
I can choose devices that suit my reader and explain their effect.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: On purpose is the key. A device should never be an accident.
SAY: Read the I can lines with me. Everyone, together, on three.
SAY: Spotting devices is where we start.
Adding one that works is today's main goal.
notes.prep: SC1 spotting devices is reachable for all; SC2 adding a device is the core and the exit evidence; SC3 choosing for the reader and naming the effect is the stretch.

slides.title: What makes this pump you up?
lines: We trained hard. We played hard. Now we finish hard.

notes.answer: the repeated pattern, we, and the question at the end
beats: SAY: A footy coach at three-quarter time. Listen.
READ it like a coach, building up.
ASK: Did that make you want to run back out?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up
ASK: What did the coach do with the words?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: said hard three times; said we; asked a question
SAY: Last week we chose powerful words.
Today we learn patterns that make words hit harder.
trap: it was loud, so it worked.
Fix: read it flat and quiet; ask what still works? Student finds the pattern.
notes.prep: Launch links Week 2 word power to devices. 3 minutes.

slides.meaning: A word pattern a writer uses on purpose to persuade.
slides.example: Asking a question you don't want answered is a device.

notes.answer: a word pattern a writer uses on purpose to persuade
beats: POINT to the word. SAY: Device. Say it with me. Device.
SAY: A device is a tool in your toolkit: a pattern used on purpose.
Like a wrench, you pick the right one for the job.
ASK: What device did the coach use most?
10 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: repeating hard
trap: thinking device means a phone or tablet.
Fix: say in writing, a device is a tool made of words.
notes.prep: The word the session runs on; the wrench makes it a tool.

slides.title: Four tools and what they do

rows: Do we really want to lose them?
makes you answer in your head
They need ice, food and space.
We can act. We can change.
puts the reader on your team

notes.answer: each device has a job: name the effect, not just the device
beats: POINT to Rhetorical question.
SAY: I don't want an answer out loud. I want you answering no in your head.
POINT to Rule of three.
SAY: Ice, food and space. Three feels complete. Two feels short.
POINT to We-words.
SAY: We, us, our. Now the reader is on my team, not being told off.
ASK: Which tool would you use to end a paragraph? Why?
15 sec. Turn and tell, partner A first.
EXPECT: a rhetorical question, it leaves them thinking
trap: naming a device but not what it does to the reader.
Fix: ask so what does it make the reader do? Student adds the effect.
notes.stretch: Find a sentence that uses two devices at once.
notes.help: Learn the rule of three first; it's the easiest to use.
notes.prep: The model. Critical feature: a device earns its place only if it moves the reader. Examples are the student's own topic language.

slides.title: Name the device
slides.pivot: check each tool on the board in order
slides.followUp: cold call one student: what does it make the reader do?

items.text: Is a few minutes of convenience worth a hundred years of rubbish?
Walking to school is cheaper, healthier and cleaner.
Every bottle counts. Every bag counts. Every choice counts.
items.say: Repetition, and three of them. Two tools at once. Tick or fix.

items.text: Together, our school can lead the way.
Who wants to breathe dirty air?

say: 1 question, 2 rule of three, 3 repetition, 4 we-words.
trap: calling any question a rhetorical question.
Fix: ask does the writer want a real answer? If not, it's rhetorical.
notes.stretch: Say the effect of each one.
notes.help: Look for a question mark, then a list, then a repeat, then we.
notes.prep: Guided naming. Item 3 is the double-device edge case. SC1.

slides.title: Which one puts the reader on your team?

options.text: Polar bears need ice, food and space to survive.
options.misconception: a rule of three; confuses any device with we-words

options.text: Together, we can protect the Arctic for good.
Can you imagine a world without any polar bears?
options.misconception: a rhetorical question; involves the reader but doesn't make them part of us

notes.answer: B - together and we put the reader on the team
beats: SAY: Three sentences, three devices. Which one makes you part of the team?
ASK: Which one puts the reader on your team?
10 sec. Cue: voices off, everyone points to A, B or C.
EXPECT: pointing to B
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, cold call: which device is A?
Less -> circle we, us, our on the board, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: B. Together and we. You're not being told off, you're being invited.
trap: pointing to C because it talks to you.
Fix: ask does it say we? Student finds the we-words in B.
notes.prep: Decision point: the device by its effect. Under 80% means the Add a device round is done in pairs first.

slides.title: Add a device
slides.pivot: build one together on the board, then re-ask
slides.followUp: cold call one board: what does your device make the reader do?

items.text: Plastic harms turtles. Add a rhetorical question.
items.answer: How many more turtles must choke on our rubbish?
items.expect: a question that wants no answer

items.text: Trees give shade. Add a rule of three.
items.answer: Trees give us shade, clean air and homes for birds.
We can all recycle, and together our school can lead the way.
Act now. Act together. Act before it's too late.

say: Your turn to use the tools.
Each sentence tells you which device to add.
trap: a rule of three with three things that mean the same, like big, huge, large.
Fix: ask are they three different reasons? Student swaps two.
notes.stretch: Add two devices to one sentence.
notes.help: Use the example in the table as a pattern.
notes.prep: Guided adding, one device each. SC2.

slides.title: Device remix
slides.task: Work through your Worksheet. Finish by remixing your Week 2 paragraph with three labelled devices.

notes.answer: a remixed paragraph with three labelled devices
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: Same paragraph, but better tools. Don't cram them all in one sentence.
SAY: Read the task, complete each part, check your work.
Finished? Extension next. Everyone, together, on three.
CIRCULATE. Ask: what does that one make your reader do?
ASK: Swap books. How many devices can you find in your partner's?
10 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest... show me.
EXPECT: 3 or more
TIME 15 minutes, including the 2-minute swap.
trap: five rhetorical questions in a row.
Fix: student keeps the best question, swaps the rest for other tools.
notes.stretch: Extension: name each device's effect, then judge which earn their place.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: picture-clue choices, a first device added, a frame.
notes.prep: Independent application on students' own Week 2 writing. SC2 and SC3.

slides.extendedTask: a worksheet ending in a paragraph remixed with three labelled devices

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Bikes are good for the planet.
Rewrite it with one device. Name the device you used.

notes.answer: e.g. Bikes are quiet, cheap and clean. Rule of three
beats: SAY: A plain sentence about something new. Use one tool.
ASK: Rewrite the sentence with a device, and name it.
60 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: a question, a three, a repeat or we-words, correctly named
RECORD who names a device that isn't there. Tomorrow's warm-up.
trap: rewriting with emotive words only and calling it a device.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new sentence. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Which tool will you use most in your big piece? Tell your partner why it suits your reader.

notes.answer: open - listen for a device matched to a reader
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together. Everyone, together, on three.
ASK: How sure are you that you can add a device on purpose?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
ASK: Which tool will you use most in your big piece, and why?
20 sec. Turn and tell, partner B first.
EXPECT: we-words, because I'm writing to the principal
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. SC2.

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Your turn: name devices, choose the right one, add devices, then remix your own paragraph.
resources.title: The Persuader's Toolkit
resources.subtitle: Use a device on purpose, for a reason.

example.prompt: 'We can do this. We can win this.'
steps: Is there a question? A list of three?

items.prompt: Name the device: rhetorical question, rule of three, repetition or we-words.
rows: Shade trees cool, protect and calm us.
Who wants a playground like an oven?
Together, our class can fix this.
Every bin matters. Every day matters.
Can we really ignore a dying reef?
answers: Shade trees cool, protect and calm us.
Who wants a playground like an oven?
Together, our class can fix this.
Every bin matters. Every day matters.
Can we really ignore a dying reef?

example.prompt: Goal: leave the reader thinking at the end.
steps: What should the reader do or feel?
example.answer: A rhetorical question: they keep answering it in their head.

items.prompt: Goal: make readers feel part of the team. Which works?
options: Together, our school can save the bees.
Why would anyone hurt a bee?
items.explain: Together and our put the reader on the writer's team.

items.prompt: Lucy tried a rule of three. Find her mistake and fix it.
work: Bees are small, little and tiny.
items.answer: All three words mean the same thing. Fix: Bees pollinate crops, make honey and feed birds.

example.prompt: Plain: Sport keeps us healthy. Add: rule of three.
example.answer: Sport keeps our hearts strong, our minds calm and our friendships close.

items.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the device named.
answers: Together, we can save every drop.
How many more animals must choke on our litter?
Walk for your health. Walk for your planet. Walk to school.

steps: Add three devices in different places
Label each device and its effect
example.answer: A remixed paragraph with three labelled devices.

items.prompt: Remix your Week 2 Prove it paragraph with three devices. Label each one in the margin with its effect.
items.answer: A remixed paragraph with three devices, each labelled with its effect.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: name each device's effect, then judge which devices earn their place.
resources.title: Toolkit Expert
resources.subtitle: A device must earn its place.

sections.title: What does it do to the reader?

steps: What does the reader feel or do?
example.answer: Repetition: it builds urgency, so the reader wants to act.

items.prompt: Name the device and its effect on the reader.
rows: Is a cheaper toy worth a dead turtle?
This is our school, our future, our choice.
answers: Is a cheaper toy worth a dead turtle?
easy steps to remember and do
This is our school, our future, our choice.

example.prompt: Too many devices: 'Why? Why? Why? We, us, our...'
steps: Write it with all four devices
example.answer: Too many devices sound like shouting; keep the ones that move the reader.

items.prompt: Write a closing paragraph using all four devices. Cross out the one that doesn't earn its place, and explain why.
items.answer: A paragraph with four devices, one crossed out, and a reason.

resources.label: Supported Worksheet
resources.description: Supported option: picture-clue choices, a first device added and a frame.
resources.title: Toolkit Helper
resources.subtitle: Four tools: a question, three things, a repeat, we-words.

items.prompt: Rewrite each sentence with the device.
answers: Trees give shade, air and homes.
items.hint: The first one is done for you.

example.answer: We can give bears their freedom. (we-words)

items.prompt: Write two sentences about your issue. Use a different device in each and name it.
